hook.text: Cassini orbited Saturn for 13 years, transforming our understanding of the ringed planet and its moons.

buildup.text: It carried the Huygens probe, which landed on Titan in 2005—the farthest landing from Earth ever.

discovery.text: Cassini found water geysers erupting from Enceladus, hinting at a warm ocean beneath its icy crust.

twist.text: Titan has lakes and rain of liquid methane—the only other world with surface liquids.

climax.text: In 2017, Cassini plunged into Saturn to avoid contaminating moons that might harbor life.

punchline.text: Thirteen years at Saturn. A grand finale dive into the clouds.

quiz.question: Why was Cassini deliberately crashed into Saturn?
options: To avoid contaminating moons like Enceladus that might have life
To collect atmospheric samples during its final descent
Its fuel ran out and it could no longer maintain orbit

details.summary: The Cassini-Huygens mission orbited Saturn for 13 years (2004-2017), transforming our understanding of the ringed planet. It discovered ocean worlds (Enceladus's water geysers, Titan's methane lakes), measured ring age and dynamics, and deployed the Huygens probe — the first landing in the outer…
details.whyItMatters: Cassini revealed Saturn's moon system as one of the most scientifically rich places in the solar system. The discovery of Enceladus's subsurface ocean made it a top target in the search for extraterrestrial life.
takeaways: Cassini orbited Saturn for 13 years making groundbreaking discoveries
It discovered Enceladus's ocean geysers and Titan's methane lakes
Huygens was the first probe to land in the outer solar system

faq.question: What did Cassini discover at Enceladus?
faq.answer: Cassini flew through geysers erupting from cracks in Enceladus's south pole, detecting water vapor, salt, silica nanoparticles, and organic molecules. This confirmed a global subsurface ocean with hydrothermal vents on the seafloor — conditions potentially suitable for life.

faq.question: Why was Cassini deliberately destroyed?
faq.answer: By 2017, Cassini was running low on fuel. Rather than risk it crashing into and contaminating potentially habitable moons (Enceladus or Titan), NASA chose a 'Grand Finale' — 22 daring orbits between Saturn and its rings, followed by a controlled plunge into Saturn's atmosphere on September 15, 2017.
